::: {.fi-standfirst}
Information can be health. Most of what we know never arrives in a form anyone can
act on, and that is a solvable problem.
:::

## Meet the person this is for

Someone in their sixties, working hard, loves their family, loves the food they grew
up on, and has just been told their blood pressure is a problem. They want to live a
healthy life. They have one real question: what should I actually do?

Where do they go?

Four things have to be true at the same time. It has to be **accurate**, or it is
worse than nothing. **Actionable**, or it changes no one's Tuesday. **Accessible**,
or it reaches only people who already had good options. And **fun**, because
attention is the currency and nobody finishes something dutiful.

| Where they turn | Accurate | Actionable | Accessible | Fun |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Primary care** | Yes, for medicine | Rarely, in fifteen minutes | Only if you have a doctor | No |
| **A dietitian** | Varies, with little measurement to work from | Yes | Costs money most will not spend twice | Sometimes |
| **The internet** | Often wrong, and paid by the click | Yes | Yes | Very |

Nobody delivers all four. Everything real gets built on the assumption that people
will tolerate boring if it is true, and they will not, and then we call that a
motivation problem.

## Discovery and delivery are supposed to be one loop

There is no shortage of health knowledge. There are over a thousand cardiovascular
risk algorithms, more than two hundred systems for defining a healthy food, and
something like half a million nutrition studies. What there is almost none of is
infrastructure for turning any of it into an honest, personal, actionable answer for
one real person making one real decision.

Delivery is the obvious half of that, and it is not the whole problem. Discovery and
delivery are supposed to run as one loop. A study becomes a guideline, a guideline
becomes something a person actually does, what happens next gets observed, and what
comes back decides which question is worth asking next. Each half is supposed to
steer the other.

The return edge is missing. [Mapping the organizations that sit between evidence and
action](../ai-for-science-map/), the last thing anyone does is revise: find out the
thing is not working, and stop. Almost nothing occupies that stage, and the reason is
structural rather than lazy. Stopping needs a rule set in advance, a rule needs to
know whether the thing is working, and that needs a benefit signal. [We built
surveillance for harm and almost none for
benefit](../we-measure-harm-we-mean-benefit/), so nothing tells you it is working,
so no stopping rule can be written, so nothing flows back into what gets studied
next.

That is why the incentive structures that produce fifty competing dietary indices
were never going to produce one useful answer. Nothing downstream was ever going to
tell them which of the fifty was worth having. The argument over what counts as
ultraprocessed is the shiniest current example: enormous political and scientific
capital spent on a definition, while the person holding a box in a grocery aisle
gets no closer to knowing what to do, and no signal returns from that aisle to say
so.

## Why nobody built it

Universities generate the knowledge that ends up in our books and our schools. Ask
almost any researcher how it is going and you will hear some version of just
surviving. The work gets produced and then it goes nowhere in particular, because
nothing orchestrates it toward the questions that matter. Articles pile up in the
tens of thousands. The incentive is the next publication, and a field can group-think
its way into an ivory tower built on a comfortable lie: that science is unbiased by
nature. It is not. Every algorithm, every risk score, every model carries somebody's
judgment inside it.

There has never been a real source of quality health information and delivery
because there has never been an incentive to build one. Not in medicine. Not in
health care. Not in the food industry. Not in prestigious academic institutions.
Nowhere.

## How I got here

I trained as a tissue engineer and spent years building multicellular experimental
models of inflammation, regeneration, and disease. Somewhere in there I became
convinced the real problem was not our ability to generate health knowledge. It was
our almost complete inability to orchestrate that generation toward questions that
matter, and then to consolidate and deliver what comes back.

So I moved sideways, into nutritional epidemiology, and then into building. I have
published in the field, worked with people who know far more than I do, and become
steadily more humbled by how hard the cultural, data, and statistical problems
actually are. Bayesian inference feels like the right home for this work, because
every algorithm, risk score, and model reflects judgment rather than fact, and I
would rather build tools that say so.

So I started building it. FRESH is my attempt at the infrastructure problem. It is
not finished, and I do not know that I am solving it correctly. I think the question
is the right one, and I would rather work on it in public than wait until I am sure.

## What honest looks like in practice

Saying how sure you are is not a disclaimer bolted on at the end. It changes what
gets built.

A number without its uncertainty is not an answer, so the doubt stays visible on the
result. Quality never collapses to a single score. When credible expert systems
disagree about the same food, the spread is reported rather than averaged away, and
the food is marked contested rather than quietly assigned a number. Contradictions
between studies get explained before they are declared. Measurement error is carried
from the raw input through to the value on screen. Nothing counts as settled here
until it reproduces a published benchmark, standard error included.

None of that is the point of the platform. It is what makes the point trustworthy.

## The information is already everywhere

Nobody sits down to consult the informational environment. It arrives anyway. It is
the conversation at dinner, the answer you give a child who asks why one cereal is
better than another, the headline you half-read on a phone, the thing a friend
swears worked for them, the label you glance at with a cart in your hand. None of it
announces itself as information. By the time anyone makes a decision, belief has
already taken shape in the background, assembled out of all of it.

That is why pointing at individual choices misreads the problem. Nobody stands
outside the information they grew up inside, experts included. So what people
believe gets measured here with the same seriousness as composition and effect
sizes, then compared against the evidence. The gaps come back specific: foods the
public judges harshly that the evidence treats kindly, foods it lets off easy, and
foods the experts cannot agree on either, which makes public confusion an entirely
reasonable response. Naming which is which is an education agenda, food by food,
rather than a scolding.

## Food first, then the rest of a life

Food comes first because it is the hardest case and the most daily one: expert
systems clash most openly there, measurement is noisiest, and public belief has
drifted furthest from the evidence. The methods are not about food. The same
machinery reaches sleep, movement, mind and mood, social connection and loneliness,
self-care, substance use, biological age, health literacy, and the place you live,
read from what you report, what you wear, and what your blood says.

## What it is made of

Five engines sit behind the tools and essays here. None of them is really about
food.

| Engine | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | Reads the published literature end to end: finds the studies, checks trial quality and trustworthiness, re-pools the effects, and keeps a trail from every claim back to its source. |
| **Consensus** | Reconciles competing expert rating systems into one answer with the disagreement measured and reported, never hidden inside an average. |
| **Risk** | Combines risk models with trial-derived effects to estimate what a change is actually worth for particular people and places, with uncertainty propagated rather than dropped. |
| **Decision** | Turns contradictory signals into one personal answer that shows its own doubt. |
| **Well-being** | Scores well-being across an open set of life domains from self-report, wearable, and biomarker inputs, per domain and combined. |

Together they are meant to do what no single adviser can, which is the framing on
the [front page](index.qmd).

## Who this is for

Anyone who wants to see the evidence for themselves: people making decisions about
their own health, the people who care for them, and the people writing the labels,
the guidance, and the policy. The essays are the argument in public. The tools let
you check it.

If you are thinking about health measurement, clinical risk, nutrition science,
science reform, or what honest evidence synthesis even looks like, I want to hear
from you. So let's start talking better, asking better questions, and building tools
that turn scientific complexity into better health decisions.
